summary: Strengthen the orbital picture and qualify how bond energies support reactivity comparisons.

improvements.where: note, Key ideas after the sigma and pi bond paragraph; teaching card 9701-3.4.2
improvements.why: Outcome 9701-3.4.2 asks how orbital overlap forms sigma and pi bonds, but the note gives only definitions and bond counts, so a learner cannot picture the geometry or explain why a pi bond restricts rotation.
improvements.what: Add a compact verbal orbital sketch for ethene: each carbon uses three $sp^2$ orbitals for end-on $\sigma$ overlap in one plane; the remaining parallel unhybridised p orbitals overlap sideways above and below that plane to make one $\pi$ bond. Contrast with the two perpendicular p-orbital overlaps in a triple bond. Keep this as prose because the supported diagram table cannot draw orbital lobes.

improvements.where: note, Key ideas and Method at hybridisation; teaching card 9701-3.4.2
improvements.why: The current rule assigns hybridisation from sigma-bond count alone; lone pairs are also electron regions, so applying it to nitrogen in ammonia would incorrectly give $sp^2$ rather than $sp^3$.
improvements.what: Add the full method: count sigma bonds plus lone pairs around the atom; 2 regions imply sp, 3 imply $sp^2$, 4 imply $sp^3$. Show that ammonia has three $\sigma$ bonds and one lone pair, hence four regions and $sp^3$, while ethene carbon has three regions and $sp^2$.

improvements.where: note, Key ideas after bond-energy comparison and Exam technique; teaching card 9701-3.4.3
improvements.why: The note states that a stronger bond makes a molecule less reactive, which is too broad for reactions involving other bonds and conditions; outcome 9701-3.4.3 calls for comparison using bond energies and bond lengths.
improvements.what: Add the qualification that bond energy predicts the relative ease of breaking the particular bond being compared, under comparable conditions; overall reactivity also depends on the reaction pathway and bonds formed. Retain the existing nitrogen/oxygen and halogen examples as comparisons of the named bond-breaking step.
